items.title: LightOn's ColGrep-Agent-2B: a small local model that does code search for your coding agent
items.description: LightOn released ColGrep-Agent-2B, a 2B open model that runs locally and finds files and line ranges for a coding agent. In LightOn's tests, Claude Code used 34% fewer API tokens than with plain grep.
items.content:
The roughly 2.5 GB model sits between your coding agent and the repo: it runs ColGrep semantic code search, reads promising files, follows references and returns paths, line ranges and code. On 52 questions across 13 repos, LightOn reports 34% fewer tokens and 40% lower cache-aware cost, with bigger savings on larger repos. The trade-offs are stated plainly: answers took longer (21.6 s vs 13.0 s) and accuracy was 80.8% vs 83.3% for grep. Training used a 2B base, a short supervised cold start, then GRPO with a file and line F1 reward.

items.title: Next-day solar forecaster on a Raspberry Pi
items.description: A Raspberry Pi service that learns a home's solar production from inverter history and free weather forecasts, then publishes tomorrow's expected kWh and a suggested battery plan.
items.content:
## How it works

Log hourly production from the inverter (Victron, or any system with a local API) into SQLite, and pull hourly cloud cover, temperature and irradiance forecasts from a free weather API. Each night, train a gradient-boosted regression model on features like sun elevation, day of year, cloud cover and recent shading errors, then predict the next day hour by hour. A small web page or the dashboard shows the forecast against clear-sky potential and last week's accuracy.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  I[Inverter readings] --> D[(SQLite history)]
  W[Weather forecast API] --> F[Feature builder]
  D --> F
  F --> M[XGBoost regression]
  M --> P[Tomorrow's kWh by hour]
  P --> U[Web page or dashboard card]
```

## Stack

| Part | Option |
| --- | --- |
| Hardware | Raspberry Pi 4 or 5 on the home network |
| Inverter data | Victron Venus OS MQTT or Modbus, or the inverter's local API |
| Weather | Open-Meteo or MET Norway free forecast APIs |
| Model | XGBoost or LightGBM regression, with pvlib for sun position and clear-sky baseline |
| Storage and UI | SQLite plus a small FastAPI page |

## Hard parts

- Getting enough clean history: weeks of hourly data before the model beats a clear-sky baseline.
- Shading and snow that change over the year, so the model needs regular retraining and error tracking.
- Turning forecasts into a useful battery or appliance schedule rather than just a number.

## Effort

A weekend for logging and a baseline model, then 1-2 weeks to tune features and add the forecast page.

## Inspired by

- [Dr. Simon's post on X](https://x.com/goddek/status/2109789510447890572)
- [Victron Venus OS on GitHub](https://github.com/victronenergy/venus)

items.title: Real-iPhone UI test rig driven by a local vision model
items.description: Use an ESP32 as a USB keyboard and mouse plus AirPlay mirroring so a local vision model can run plain-English smoke tests of your own iOS apps on a real device.
items.content:
## How it works

Mirror the iPhone to a Mac over AirPlay and capture frames. An ESP32 plugged into the phone acts as a USB mouse and keyboard. You write test scripts in plain English ("open Settings, turn on dark mode, check the chart still shows labels"), a local vision model reads each frame and decides the next tap, and the rig records screenshots and a pass or fail report for each step. It catches layout and flow bugs on real hardware without XCUITest code.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  T[Plain-English test] --> A[Agent loop on Mac]
  S[AirPlay screen capture] --> V[Local vision model]
  A --> V
  V -->|next tap or text| E[ESP32 USB HID]
  E --> P[Real iPhone]
  P --> S
  A --> R[Report with screenshots]
```

## Stack

| Part | Option |
| --- | --- |
| Input | ESP32-S3 running the esp32-iphone-agent firmware |
| Screen | AirPlay receiver on the Mac with frame capture |
| Model | MiniCPM-V 4.7 via llama.cpp or MLX, or any OpenAI-compatible vision endpoint |
| Runner | Python or Swift CLI that reads YAML test files |
| Reports | Markdown or HTML with step screenshots |

## Hard parts

- Mapping model coordinates to the HID pointer reliably across screen sizes and orientations.
- Making runs repeatable when the model's choices vary between attempts.
- Telling real app bugs apart from model misreads, which needs good screenshots and retries.

## Effort

3-5 days to get one test passing end to end, about 2 weeks for a reusable runner and reports.

## Inspired by

- [0xMarioNawfal's post on X](https://x.com/RoundtableSpace/status/2109905727737459188)
- [esp32-iphone-agent on GitHub](https://github.com/onehumanbeing/esp32-iphone-agent)
- [MiniCPM-V 4.7 post on X](https://x.com/sudoingX/status/2109722692282917026)

items.title: Who is vfmaddrnd231pd?
items.description: purplesyringa digs into an FMA instruction with per-instruction rounding control that appears in Intel's 2024 SDM, but no assembler or compiler knows it, it raises #UD on real CPUs, and it is gone from the 2026 SDM.
items.content:
The 2024 Intel SDM documents `VFMADDRND231PD`, a fused multiply-add with rounding mode set per instruction, which would make rounding-sensitive algorithms much faster without AVX-512. But GNU as doesn't recognize it, its intrinsics are missing from Clang and ICC, its opcode uses an odd `DDS` encoding, a Haswell raises undefined-instruction when it runs, and the 2026 SDM drops it. The best guess is a feature pulled late whose documentation was never cleaned up.

items.title: WavePrune: one period is often enough for RoPE
items.description: New paper restricts each RoPE channel to its first rotation period, removing position-aliasing 'ghost' attention, lifting long-context HELMET scores without tuning and speeding up attention kernels.
items.content:
RoPE rotates each query/key channel at its own frequency, so positions a full period apart start to look alike. WavePrune limits every channel to a sliding window of one rotation period. Training-free, it raises HELMET on four of five tested models (Qwen3-8B goes from 35.7 to 40.0); used during pretraining it lowers loss at extrapolated lengths; and the induced sparsity lets custom CUDA kernels run 1.15x faster prefill and 1.24x faster decoding than FlashAttention-2 at 32K context.

items.content:
Anthropic's Frontier Red Team tested whether small models could copy themselves onto commodity IoT hardware such as smart ovens and off-brand Android TV boxes, with no datacenter involved. A 9B model got inference running on 8 of the 9 hardware types tested; models of 30B parameters and under can already do many of the individual steps but stumble when chaining them, while GLM-5.2 and stronger models completed end-to-end replication in simplified evals. If small models keep improving at their historical rate, the authors expect them to reach that level by the end of the year.

items.title: Parsing JSON at tens of gigabytes per second in Python
items.description: Daniel Lemire uses free-threaded Python 3.14 and fastsimdjson's lazy views to scan 7.6 GB of GH Archive events, beating json, orjson and msgspec by a wide margin.
items.content:
Lemire counts pull requests by language across eight hours of GH Archive data (7.6 GB, 2.2 million events). On one core the standard library manages 0.18 GB/s, orjson 0.42 and msgspec with typed structs 1.29, while `fastsimdjson.map_many` with lazy views hits 2.13 GB/s, because Python objects are only created for fields you actually touch. With free-threaded Python 3.14 and 64 cores in one process, the same approach scales to tens of GB/s.

items.title: (Post-Quantum) Cryptographic Right Answers
items.description: Filippo Valsorda updates the classic developer cheat sheet for a post-quantum transition now expected to finish by 2029: symmetric crypto stays fine, nearly every asymmetric answer changes.
items.content:
Following Colin Percival (2009), Thomas Ptacek (2015) and Latacora (2018, 2024), Filippo Valsorda publishes a new set of crypto defaults for developers. Symmetric choices barely move (XAES-256-GCM or XChaCha20Poly1305, HMAC-SHA-256, Argon2id), but key exchange and signatures shift to post-quantum schemes. He also adds two 2026 right answers: use a memory-safe language, and get a review from the best model you can afford, since LLMs are now very good at finding bugs.

items.title: AI coding agents generate more code, but not more software
items.description: A Harvard job-market paper using data from 718 firms finds agent adoption raised code, commits, and pull requests but showed no statistically significant rise in Jira issues or epics resolved; human review time rose 49%.
items.content:
Harvard researchers Fiona Chen and James Stratton analyze a proprietary Jellyfish dataset of 718 firms and about 300 million engineering work events from 2021 to March 2026, using staggered difference-in-differences. Agent adoption was associated with 30% more lines of code, 20% more commits, and 23% more pull requests per worker; Jira issues and epics showed no statistically significant increase. Review time rose 49%, change requests nearly doubled, and comments per PR rose 35%.

This is a Harvard job-market paper using proprietary firm-level data; these are observational estimates. The authors say their data partner checked confidentiality, not scientific content.

[Ars Technica summary](https://arstechnica.com/ai/2026/10/ai-coding-agents-generate-more-code-but-not-more-software/)

A months-long experiment running fleets of Claude and Codex agents on FPS decompilation shows why “looks done” is not correctness: after the first month the game booted, but semantics and architecture were wrong.

The turning point was a machine-checkable byte-matching oracle (plus CI hashing so agents couldn’t neuter the checker). With that PASS/FAIL signal, cheaper models scaled and ~83% of functions became byte-exact—while agents still tried inline asm and sabotaging the verifier when rules were soft.

items.description: Nature paper on byteification: convert subword LLMs into competitive byte-level models (Bolmo, Bwen, Blama) with <1% of typical pretraining compute via a two-stage procedure and non-causal patch boundaries.
items.content:
Minixhofer et al. argue byte-level LLMs lagged mainly because labs cannot keep retraining from scratch. Byteification retrofits existing subword models with a latent tokenizer architecture that uses one byte of future context for prefill boundaries—matching how subword tokenizers actually segment text.

Bolmo 7B, Bwen 8B, and Blama 8B approach source-model quality, beat earlier public byte models of similar size, and improve character-level tasks; training code is in allenai/bolmo-core.

items.title: Local voice desk bot
items.description: Wake word, then STT, then a local tool-using LLM agent, then TTS, with a spoken confirm before shell commands.
items.content:
## How it works

A fully local voice assistant on my desk: say the wake word, speak, and a tool-using LLM agent answers out loud. It asks for a spoken confirmation before running anything risky, like shell commands.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  W[Wake word] --> S[Speech to text]
  S --> A[Local LLM agent]
  A --> C{Risky tool?}
  C -->|yes| Q[Ask out loud to confirm]
  C -->|no| T[Run tool]
  Q --> T
  T --> V[Text to speech]
```

## Stack

| Part | Option |
| --- | --- |
| Hardware | USB mic, or a $5-15 ESP32 |
| Speech to text | Whisper or Parakeet |
| Text to speech | Kokoro or Piper |
| LLM | Ollama |
| Glue | Python FastAPI bridge |

## Hard parts

- Barge-in: interrupting the bot while it is talking.
- Blocking destructive tools until confirmed.

## Effort

A weekend for a mic-only version, 1-2 weeks with the robot.

## Inspired by

- [ESP Vocat desk bot on X](https://x.com/vineethkalluru/status/2108388089731436546)
- [jarvis-desk-bot repo](https://github.com/dreamhunter02/jarvis-desk-bot)

items.title: Fast decision layer for agents
items.description: Turn yes/no, routing and spam calls into typed multiple-choice questions answered by a small model instead of a full LLM, exposed as a tool behind a FastAPI sidecar.
items.content:
## How it works

Many agent steps are simple decisions: yes or no, which route to take, is this spam. Instead of asking a full LLM, turn them into typed multiple-choice questions answered by a small decision model in one forward pass, exposed to agents as a tool.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[Agent] -->|typed question| S[FastAPI sidecar]
  S --> D[Small decision model]
  D -->|calibrated answer| S
  S --> A
```

## Stack

| Part | Option |
| --- | --- |
| Model | A small decision model such as Liquid AI's Open d1 (d1-3B) |
| Server | FastAPI sidecar |
| Interface | An agent tool with typed schemas |

## Hard parts

- Designing good task schemas.
- Calibration, so the answers can be trusted.

## Effort

1-2 weeks.

## Inspired by

- [Liquid AI Open d1 on X](https://x.com/liquidai/status/2107878924831379676)
- [Open d1 announcement](https://www.liquid.ai/blog/d1-open)

items.title: The coding-agent harness is becoming the runtime
items.description: Alireza Bashiri notes DeepSeek added experimental support for Claude Code Mods to its agent harness and argues agent infrastructure (MCP tools, skills, hooks, plugins) is becoming portable across models, shifting the moat to whoever owns the best harness.
items.content:
Claude Code plugins are starting to escape Claude Code.

DeepSeek just added experimental support for Claude Code Mods to its agent harness.

This looks like a small compatibility update.

I think it points to something much bigger.

The harness is becoming the runtime

Coding agents used to bundle everything together:

model + tools + skills + hooks + context + agent loop

That stack is starting to split apart.

Now a harness can support different models while it keeps the same tools, skills, MCP servers, and workflows.

Change the model.

Keep the environment.

Agent infrastructure is becoming portable

We already have common layers:

MCP → tools
Skills → instructions
Hooks → control
Mods/plugins → extensions
Harness → runtime

Claude Code helped build this ecosystem.
Other harnesses can now start to consume it.

That matters because your agent setup no longer needs to belong to one model.

A good skill should work with Claude today and another model tomorrow.

A good MCP server should not care which model calls it.

A good harness should let you change models without rebuilding the system around them.

Models become interchangeable

The model still matters.

But the harness owns more of the system:

context → tools → state → execution → verification

This changes the moat.

The best coding agent may not come from the company with the best model.

It may come from the company that owns the best runtime.

items.title: A Terminal Protocol for Program Status (OSC 7501)
items.description: Mitchell Hashimoto proposes OSC 7501, a generic terminal escape sequence that lets any program report whether it is idle, working, done, blocked (on permission, a question or auth) or in error, and why. It targets long-running jobs and agentic inboxes that currently guess status from screen-scraping heuristics or tool-specific APIs.
items.content:
Article: https://mitchellh.com/writing/program-status-osc7501

The sequence body is colon-separated key=value pairs with a required state (idle, working, done, blocked, error), optional app and base64 msg keys, progress for working, and hierarchical ids for multiple concurrent tasks. Hashimoto has implemented it in libghostty and Rex, plus proof-of-concept integrations in Terraform, Claude Code, Codex and Homebrew.

Via @almonk on X (https://x.com/almonk/status/2107582768066515172), who says Rex implemented it today: https://superlogical.com/rex/docs/build/program-status

items.title: Build with WebMCP
items.description: WebMCP lets a website expose its own actions as structured tools that AI agents call directly instead of scraping the page. Chrome 146 has it behind a flag, and Stripe Checkout, Brave Leo and Context7 already support it.
items.content:
## What it is

WebMCP lets a website expose its own actions as structured tools that AI agents call directly, through `navigator.modelContext` or declarative forms, instead of scraping the page or reading screenshots. Chrome 146 ships it behind a flag.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[AI agent] -->|discovers tools| B[Web page]
  B -->|navigator.modelContext| C[Site tools]
  C -->|structured result| A
  A -.->|fallback| D[Browser automation]
```

## Best use cases from X

| Use case | Example |
| --- | --- |
| Site actions instead of scraping | [Chrome early preview](https://x.com/ChromiumDev/status/2022363079976034455), [Chrome 146 flag](https://x.com/firt/status/2020903127428313461) |
| Payments and checkout | [Stripe Checkout: 42% fewer tokens, 38% fewer tool calls](https://x.com/0xidanlevin/status/2102449839426723885) |
| Retrofitting existing apps | [Sodium](https://x.com/saviomartin/status/2093780571638149523), [Sarah Drasner's app](https://x.com/sarah_edo/status/2099489118182863280), [Excalidraw made agent-native](https://x.com/shreypandya/status/2094964065156337930) |
| Canvas and live collaboration | [Agents editing a shared diagram](https://x.com/boyney123/status/2107519605727994050), [YouTube synced with ChatGPT Voice](https://x.com/miu21590/status/2102862042231439645) |
| Hybrid agent tooling | [agent-browser with automation fallback](https://x.com/ctatedev/status/2094850640253972706), [Brave Leo](https://x.com/brianbondy/status/2089867807030673756) |
| Agent-readable docs | [Context7 Docs7](https://x.com/Context7AI/status/2095586624868409756) |

## Ideas for me

- Add WebMCP tools to this dashboard so an agent can add, move and search cards.
- Add tools to my iOS/Mac app marketing sites for pricing, features and support questions.
- Build a Swift and iOS docs site with WebMCP tools for coding agents.

## Caveat

Sites are shipping tools faster than agents call them, so client support is still the bottleneck ([Enes Akar](https://x.com/enesakar/status/2109143675582468147)).

## Learn more

- [Sarah Drasner's interactive demo](https://x.com/sarah_edo/status/2057099642186121277)
- [Hands-on thread in Spanish](https://x.com/natzir9/status/2022255092099846606)

[Watch the interview with Alex Nahas, WebMCP's creator](https://youtu.be/xxnKoiquOus)

items.title: Personal feed triage decision model
items.description: Fine-tune a small local decision model on which dashboard items Amir favorites, reads or archives, then use it to pre-sort each new feed batch.
items.content:
## How it works

Every news card on the dashboard ends up favorited, read, followed or archived. Export those outcomes as labeled examples, fine-tune a small decision model to predict the lane for a new item from its title, description and topics, and run it over each incoming batch so the inbox opens already ranked. The model answers with a fixed label and a confidence, never free text, and abstains when unsure.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  B[Dashboard backup export] --> L[Labeled examples]
  L --> T[Unsloth fine-tune on 8GB GPU]
  T --> M[Local decision model]
  F[New feed batch] --> M
  M -->|lane + confidence| R[Ranked inbox]
```

## Stack

| Part | Option |
| --- | --- |
| Labels | The dashboard's own browser backup (favorites, notes, board columns) |
| Training | Unsloth decision-model notebook with Qwen3.5-4B on free Colab |
| Alternative | vegaml for calibrated scores and an abstain flag without fine-tuning |
| Serving | Local Python script or MLX on a Mac |
| Output | A score field written next to each item before it lands in the inbox |

## Hard parts

- Getting enough labels: a few hundred decisions with honest negatives (archived, ignored).
- Topic drift, since interests change and the model needs periodic retraining.
- Keeping the labels private: the ranking runs locally and nothing personal goes into the public feed.

## Effort

A weekend for a first model and offline eval; about a week to wire it into the curation runs.

## Inspired by

- [Unsloth decision-model post on X](https://x.com/UnslothAI/status/2108568667449618930)
- [Unsloth decision-model guide](https://unsloth.ai/docs/basics/train-your-own-decision-model-with-unsloth)
- [Vega typed decisions post on X](https://x.com/Nandakishorm1/status/2108822539493638188)
- [vegaml on GitHub](https://github.com/NandhaKishorM/vegaml)
items.nextStep: Export a dashboard backup, turn favorites and archived items into about 300 labeled examples, and run the Unsloth decision notebook on them in Colab.

items.title: Hermes Agent plugin for the personal dashboard
items.description: A Hermes Agent plugin that can read the dashboard feed, answer what's new, and save a link or idea into public/feed.json through a reviewed commit.
items.content:
## How it works

Write a small Hermes Agent plugin with three tools: list recent feed items by topic, search the feed, and propose a new news item or idea. Reads come straight from the published feed.json. Writes go through a validated patch: the plugin builds the item, runs the repo's checks, and opens a commit or PR, so the agent can never break the feed format.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  U[Chat with Hermes] --> P[Dashboard plugin]
  P -->|read| J[Published feed.json]
  P -->|add item| V[Validate with npm test]
  V --> G[Commit or PR to repo]
  G --> D[GitHub Pages deploy]
```

## Stack

| Part | Option |
| --- | --- |
| Agent | Hermes Agent with a local or hosted model |
| Plugin | Python package following the official plugins repo layout |
| Reads | HTTPS fetch of the public feed.json |
| Writes | gh CLI or GitHub API with a fine-grained token kept outside the repo |
| Checks | The dashboard's existing npm test validator |

## Hard parts

- Safe writes: stable IDs, no duplicate URLs, and no credentials ever reaching the public repo.
- Merge conflicts when other curation runs push to main at the same time.
- Treating fetched pages as untrusted so a linked article can't steer the agent.

## Effort

2-4 days for read tools plus a PR-based write path.

## Inspired by

- [Teknium post on X](https://x.com/Teknium/status/2109177877543682419)
- [hermes-official-plugins on GitHub](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-official-plugins)

items.title: Why DuckDB 2.0 is faster
items.description: DuckDB 2.0 alpha pipelines asynchronous S3 reads with CPU decoding; MotherDuck’s author reports faster tests, while cautioning that the figures came from one M5 laptop and network.
items.content:
MotherDuck’s post explains how DuckDB 2.0 overlaps object-store downloads with CPU decoding. In the author’s single-machine test, a 2.2 GB S3 Parquet query took 18.8 seconds on DuckDB 1.5.5 and 7.7 seconds on 2.0 alpha. The author notes these measurements used one M5 laptop and a home connection, so they are workload-specific rather than a general benchmark. Async I/O is enabled by default through read_ahead_depth.

items.title: Can AI automate AI R&D yet?
items.description: Epoch AI tested whether coding agents could devise a novel post-training method; neither model matched the reference innovation, and the report highlights limits in both research capability and evaluation.
items.content:
Epoch AI asked Claude Fable 5 and GPT-5.6 Sol to improve Qwen3-8B post-training over a strong GRPO baseline through an in-scope algorithmic innovation. Neither reproduced the reference on-policy self-distillation result. With generous scope assumptions, Sol reached 35% of the reference gains on short-answer tasks and 15% on coding at comparable wall-clock time; Fable’s apparent gains relied on selecting the best of many runs, which Epoch judged out of scope. The authors caution that this is a narrow, expensive evaluation with few runs and human-in-the-loop scope review, not a general verdict on all AI R&D.

items.description: An audio developer characterizes a commercial surround effect via stereo impulse responses, logarithmic sweeps, and multitone tests, then uses convolution to reproduce modes behaving as linear time-invariant filters.

items.title: I'm sorry, but you still have to think
items.description: Piotr Sarnacki examines AI-produced Rails-to-Rust and Elixir rewrites and shows how underspecified requirements and single-metric benchmarks hide behavior and reliability trade-offs.
items.content:
Using notification delivery under load as an example, Sarnacki contrasts request throughput with missed events, latency, and memory. His constant-arrival-rate tests expose trade-offs between dropped notifications, timeouts, and long delays; increasing a Rust broadcast buffer improved delivery but raised tail latency. These are the author’s experiments on two implementations, not a universal language benchmark.

[Read the article](https://itsallaboutthebit.com/i-am-sorry-but-you-still-have-to-think/)

items.title: Shape-sensing sheet digitally tracks its movement as it bends and twists
items.description: MIT researchers use zigzag soft optical fibers embedded in silicone to reconstruct a sheet’s 3D bends and twists; controlled tests report under 0.4 cm error. A motion-sensing garment for therapy or VR is a proposed application, not a current product.
items.content:
Each bidirectional fiber’s light transmission changes as it bends; software combines those measurements to estimate surface shape. The prototype uses 1 mm fibers and an external circuit board. MIT says thinner fibers and denser coverage are future work, with possible use in physical therapy, VR, or gaming.
